list.listitem: Avoid unnecessary catheterization and remove a urinary catheter as soon as possible to decrease the incidence of UTI. A
The USPSTF recommends that all pregnant women be screened for and treated for asymptomatic bacteriuria in early pregnancy.A

Nitrofurantoin 100 mg for 5 days or TMP-SMX 160/800 mg) twice daily for 3 days are the first-line treatments of choice for acute uncomplicated cystitis in women. Alternatives include fosfamycin, a quinolone, pivmecillinam, or amoxi-clav. A
Cranberry juice is effective in primary prevention in non-pregnant women A and secondary prevention B of symptomatic UTI.

background.definition: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is a general term used to describe infection anywhere in the urinary system: urethra, bladder (cystitis), ureters, and kidneys (pyelonephritis). Uncomplicated UTI is an infection in a healthy patient with a structurally and functionally normal urinary tract. Complicated UTI is an infection in a patient with a structural or functional abnormality of the urinary tract, immunocompromise, or infection with high-virulence bacteria. Most UTIs in men are complicated.

list.listitem: The annual incidence of UTI is 12.6%/year in women and 3%/year in men.
The peak incidence is 18.6%/year at 20 to 24 years of age in women and 7.3%/year over age 84 in men.
7 million episodes of acute cystitis and 250,000 episodes of acute pyelonephritis per year in the United States.
Prevalence of asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnant women: 1.9% to 9.5%.
In women with diabetes it is 11% to 16%, and in men with diabetes 1% to 11%. It is similar in community-dwelling elderly. In residents of long-term care facilities it is between 15% and 50%.
Uncomplicated UTI: E. coli (68%-89%), Staphylococcus saprophyticus (0%-8%), Proteus (4%-6%), Klebsiella (4%), Enterococci (0%-3%), and mixed (3%-5%).
Complicated UTI and catheter-associated UTIs: E. coli (24%-32%), Proteus (4%-6%), Klebsiella (5%-8%), Enterococci (7%-22%), Pseudomonas (9%-20%), mixed (10%-11%), and yeast (8%-15%).

Coliform organisms from the perirectal area colonize the vagina and the periurethral area. These organisms ascend the urethra to the bladder and stimulate a host response causing cystitis. If the bacteria ascend to the kidneys and stimulate a host response they cause pyelonephritis.
Adherence is an important factor for colonization of the vagina and the periurethral area and to resist the flushing action of bladder emptying.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is caused by E. coli strains that do not activate a host response or cause disease.

Pyelo-nephrogenic E. coli are of certain O and K serotypes that are different from those causing asymptomatic bacteriuria. They have P and type 1 fimbriae that are necessary for adherence to the uroepithelium. The P fimbriae exhibit strong epidemiological associations with pyelonephritis.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Insulin treated diabetes in postmenopausal women
Recent use of diaphragm and spermicide in young women
Diabetes mellitus with indwelling urinary catheter
Male sex with indwelling urinary catheter
Use of an SGLT2 inhibitor for treatment of T2DM (empagliflozin, canagliflozin)

list.listitem: The USPSTF recommends screening pregnant women for and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria. It recommends against screening non-pregnant adults.A
Screen for and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in men undergoing transurethral resection of prostate or other urologic procedure for which mucosal bleeding is expected. A
Cranberry juice or concentrates decrease the incidence and recurrence of symptomatic UTI in sexually active women (but not in pregnant women). B
Postcoital voiding does not prevent UTI in sexually active women. B
Avoid unnecessary catheterization, remove catheters as soon as possible, and use antibiotic prophylaxis at the time of removal. A
The USPSTF recommends screening pregnant women for and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria. It recommends against screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria non-pregnant adults.A

Screen for and treat UTI in patients undergoing transurethral resection of the prostate, patients undergoing urological procedures in which mucosal bleeding is anticipated, and women with catheter-acquired bacteriuria that persists for 48 hours after removal.
Do not screen for or teat asymptomatic bacteriuria in the elderly, individuals with diabetes, or patients with indwelling catheters.
In hospitalized women, finding white blood cells is not a good predictor of positive culture or infection in the absence of typical symptoms.

Cranberry juice reduces the incidence of symptomatic UTIs in sexually active women. A Cochrane review of 50 RCTs with 8857 participants found that cranberry products significantly reduce the risk of UTI cranberry products reduced the risk of UTIs (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.58 - 0.84). This was also true in women with recurrent UTIs (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.55 - 0.99) and in children (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.32 - 0.68).
However, cranberry capsules were not cost-effective as a way to prevent UTI in long term care facilities.

An RCT randomized 140 premenopausal women with 3 or more episodes of lower UTI in the past year. They were randomized to an additional 1.5 liters of water daily or usual practice for one year. The women receiving extra water had significantly fewer UTIs (1.7 vs 3.2, p <0.001).

Avoiding unnecessary catheterization and removing the catheter as soon as possible decreases the incidence of UTI. A meta-analysis concluded that one to three doses of antibiotic at the time of shorter-term (<14 days) catheter removal significantly reduced the likelihood of infection (NNT = 17).

An RCT (n = 418) found that a multimodal intervention incorporating barrier precautions, active surveillance, and staff education reduced the prevalence of multidrug resistant organisms and UTIs in long term care facility residents.
The use of antimicrobial-impregnated urinary catheters is not associated with the prevention of UTIs among hospitalized patients.
In a randomized trial of 83 persons with neurogenic bladder caused by spina bifida, single use catheters (compared with multiple use catheters) did not reduce the incidence of UTI.

A Cochrane review concluded that the evidence was inconclusive regarding the benefit of single use versus multiple use catheters, aseptic versus clean technique, uncoated versus hydrophilic coated catheters, and short versus long catheters.

A randomized trial compared parenteral cefuroxime with placebo as prophylaxis prior to 555 men not at high risk for infection undergoing transperineal prostate biopsy. Sepsis or UTI requiring hospitalization did not occur in any men, and UTI not requiring hospitalization occurred in 1 patient in the antibiotic group and 3 in the placebo group (difference -0.73%, 95% CI -1.08% to 2.81%).
Daily d-mannose did not prevent recurrent UTI in an RCT with 598 women with frequent UTIs.

A systematic review identified 8 studies of increased fluid intake to prevent recurrent UTI. It was borderline effective overall (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.15-1.03); the benefit was larger and statistically significant when studies prescribing volumes less than 200 ml daily were excluded (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.11-0.59). However, there was no impact on antimicrobial use.
Cranberry-lingo berry juice decreases the recurrence of symptomatic UTI in young women.
Postcoital voiding does not prevent UTI. However, postcoital prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin or TMP-SMX does reduce the risk of recurrent UTI in women.
Self-diagnosis and self-treatment is safe and effective for recurrent uncomplicated UTIs in young women.

Continuous prophylaxis with daily antibiotics is safe and effective in reducing the recurrence of UTI in women (NNT = 1.8). The most common side effects are vaginal and oral candidiasis, skin rash, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Continuous prophylaxis for 15 years does not increase drug resistance to ampicillin or nitrofurantoin, but resistance to TMP-SMX increases over 5 years.

A systematic review identified 12 studies comparing nitrofurantoin with other antibiotics for the prevention of recurrent UTI in women. Efficacy was similar to other antibiotics, but GI adverse effects were somewhat more common with nitrofurantoin.
Topically applied intravaginal estrogen reduces the recurrence of UTIs in postmenopausal women.
A study in women undergoing pelvic reconstructive surgery (n = 159) found that daily nitrofurantoin did not reduce the likelihood of post-operative UTI.

A systematic review identified 6 RCTs with 557 women comparing methenamine hippurate prophylaxis with either placebo or antibiotic for the prevention of recurrent UTI in women. While inconclusive, strong trends favored methenamine.

A study randomized 174 women age 18 to 45 with at least 3 uncomplicated UTIs in the past year to oral probiotic, vaginal probiotic, both, or placebos. At 4 months, a symptomatic UTI had occurred in 70% in the placebo group, 61% in the oral probiotic group, 41% in the vaginal probiotic group, and 32% in the group that received both. The differences between placebo only and the active treatments were statistically significant for the vaginal and vaginal plus oral probiotic groups. Results at 12 months were similar, with rates of UTI of 95%, 77%, 61%, and 55%, respectively.
A definitive diagnosis is not required prior to treatment for otherwise healthy women with typical symptoms of UTI who are without vaginal symptoms. B
Negative nitrites and leukocyte esterase on urine dipstick rules out UTI in pregnant women and there is no need for urine culture. B
UTI in men should be confirmed with a urinalysis and culture; a colony count ≥1,000 CFU/ml in clean-catch mid-stream-void urine sample confirms this diagnosis. C
Symptomatic lower UTI in young women is confirmed by a colony count ≥100 CFU/ml coliform in clean-catch midstream-void urine sample. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Vaginal discharge; can also have itching, odor

Differential.Differential_Name: Sexually transmitted disease (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae)
Differential.Differential_Features: Vaginal discharge, penile discharge; often purulent

list.listitem: A positive urine culture in women with acute uncomplicated cystitis is defined as a colony count ≥1,000 CFU/ml of the same uropathogen in a clean-catch mid-stream urine sample.
Colony count ≥10,000 CFU/ml of the same uropathogen in a clean-catch mid-stream urine sample is the diagnostic criterion for UTI in men and for acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria is defined as a colony count ≥100,000 CFU/ml in two consecutive clean-catch voided urine specimens in asymptomatic women; a colony count ≥100,000 CFU/ml in a single clean-catch voided urine sample in asymptomatic men; or colony count ≥100 CFU/ml in a single catheterized urine in asymptomatic men or women.

Symptoms of acute cystitis include dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, and hematuria. The probability of UTI in women presenting with one or more symptoms is 48% (95% CI 41%-55%). Self diagnosis is quite accurate to both rule-in and rule-out UTI.

The presence of dysuria and frequency without vaginal discharge or irritation increases the post-test probability to 96% (LR+ 24.6) allowing empirical treatment without urine culture. The presence of vaginal discharge or vaginal irritation substantially reduces the probability of UTI and necessitates a pelvic exam and urine culture.
In contrast to women, men with single signs or symptoms including hematuria, offensive urine odor, or nausea have a high likelihood of UTI.
Twenty five percent of elderly patients with bacteremic UTI present with pulmonary symptoms and only 63% present with fever.
Fever and chills, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, and nausea/vomiting (in the presence or absence of cystitis symptoms) suggest acute pyelonephritis.

Approximately 1-in-7 hospitalized women and 1-in-38 hospitalized men walk around with pyuria without bacterial infection. Pyuria, identified in this study by microscopy, is not a good indicator of bacteria in hospitalized people with suspected urinary tract infection; even at a cutoff of 25 cells/high-power field, only approximately half the patients will subsequently have a positive culture.
Urine dipstick can often be used in place of microscopy and urine culture for the diagnosis of UTI in women. A clean-catch urine specimen is not necessary in women.
In symptomatic women, a positive leukocyte esterase or nitrite or both (LR+ 45) increases the posttest probability to 80% or more, so empiric therapy should be considered without urine culture.

A negative result on urine dipstick in a symptomatic patient does not rule out UTI. However, a negative result for both nitrite and LE rules out infection in children, pregnant women, elderly, surgery or urology populations and there is no need for urine culture or treatment.

UA and urine culture should be ordered to confirm the diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis, UTI in men, and in patients suspected of having complicated UTI. In men, a colony count ≥1,000 CFU/ml of midstream urine has a sensitivity and specificity of 97% for UTI, whereas in women even using a colony count of ≥100,000 identifies only 51% of bladder infection with coliform bacteria. Midstream urine cultures with any evidence of Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae strongly suggest a true infection, while the presence of enterococci and group B streptococci has little predictive value.

A study found that a higher cutoff of approximately 250 leukocytes per microliter was optimal for women over the age of 65 years (88% sens, 88% spec, LR+ 7.3, LR- 0.14). The usual cutoff of > 10 leukocytes/mcl was 100% sensitive but only 36% specific.

A study identified 3392 adult inpatients with UA including microscopy and culture; patients with indwelling catheters were excluded. A negative LE and less than 5 WBC/HPF, and especially both, helps rule out UTI in hospitalized adults (NPV 95% to 97%). The NPV is somewhat lower for women 65 years and older. Only about one-third of patients with pyuria or positive LE are ultimately given a diagnosis of UTI. Positive nitrite and more than 50 bacteria/HPF had the highest PPV (43% and 41%, respectively).

The presence of squamous epithelial cells in urine microscopy has been proposed as a way to identify contamination. A study of 19,328 patients who had both microscopy and culture found that the presence of SECs was only somewhat predictive of contamination (area under the ROC curve 0.68).
The use of urine collection devices (Peezy, Whiz Midstream) did not affect the rate of contamination or any other outcomes in a randomized trial.

Blood cultures have been traditionally recommended for hospitalized patients with acute pyelonephritis. However, they are not routinely recommended because their positive yield is only 10% to 29% and the results have no influence on clinical management.
In a group of 229 older hospitalized patients with pyuria on urinalysis, procalcitonin was found to be unhelpful for diagnosing urinary tract infection.

Imaging is recommended in women with acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis only if there are symptoms of renal colic or a Renal stone is present on a plain film, the patient remains febrile after 72 hours, the infecting organism is an unusual organism, or there is rapid relapse with the same organism after stopping antibiotics. Imaging is also indicated in the management of men with recurrent lower urinary tract infections, all men with first episode of acute pyelonephritis, patients who are immunocompromised, patients with diabetes, or patients with suspected complicated UTI.

CT is superior to intravenous urography and ultrasound for detecting parenchymal abnormalities caused by infection, delineating the extent of the disease, and detecting perinephric collections. Unenhanced CT is superior for detecting calculi, gas performing infections, obstruction, and hemorrhage. A contrast-enhanced study will detect abnormalities in perfusion and excretion. There is universal agreement that CT is the imaging of choice ito diagnose patients with atypical pyelonephritis or to look for complications of infection.

Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography with the contrast pulse-sequence was found to be as accurate as contrast-enhanced CT in detecting renal parenchymal changes in acute pyelonephritis (sensitivity 98%, specificity 100%, positive predicitve value 100%, negative predictive value 89%).
Two clinical decision rules, by Wigton and Leibovici, have been proposed and validated.
Both use a combination of signs, symptoms, and findings on microscopic urinalysis to stratify patients into different risk groups for UTI.
Another algorithm uses procalcitonin to identify patients benefiting from an antibiotic, and was able to reduce antibiotic use without increase complication rates.
Machine learning algorithms (one requiring microscopy, one not) had excellent accuracy for diagnosis of UTI in adults in both ED and primary care settings.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to the patient with suspected UTI.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to the patient with recurrent UTI.
Mitterberger M, Pinggera GM, Colleselli D, et al. Acute pyelonephritis: Comparison of diagnosis with computed tomography and contrast-enhanced ultrasonography.
Symptomatic women with frequency and dysuria but without vaginal discharge should get empirical therapy for uncomplicated UTI without the need for urine culture. A

Physicians should know local resistance patterns. Nitrofurantoin 100 mg for 5 days or TMP-SMX 160/800 mg) twice daily for 3 days are recommended as the first-line treatments of choice for acute uncomplicated cystitis in women. Recommended alternatives include fosfamycin or pivmecillinam. Fluoroquinolones should not be used as first line therapy.A

A 14-day course of oral fluoroquinolone is the preferred drug for outpatient treatment of mild cases of pyelonephritis in women. Patients with severe pyelonephritis should be hospitalized and treated with IV antibiotics. B
Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy decreases the risk of pyelonephritis and low-birth weight infants. A

listitem.strong: Uncomplicated lower tract UTI in women

list.listitem: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) 160/800 mg twice daily for 3 days and nitrofurantoin 100 mg once daily for 5 days are the recommended first-line agents for treatment of uncomplicated cystitis in non-allergic women with no recent hospitalization, no current use of antibiotics, no use of TMP-SMX in the past 3 months. E coli resistance for TMP-SMX has been increasing in some communities, and some guidelines (based on expert opinion and modeling) recommend that it should not be used when resistance exceeds 20% in your community.

Fosfomycin trometamol (3 grams in a single dose) and pivmecillinam are also good choices for first-line therapy. However, in a randomized trial in 513 adult women with uncomplicated UTI, nitrofurantoin was significantly more likely than fosfamycin to result in clinical resolution at 28 days (70% vs 58%, NNT = 8).
On the other hand, a meta-analysis of 15 studies with 1976 patients found no difference bertween fosfomycin and a variety of comparator antibiotics for the outcome of clinical resolution.

Fluoroquinolone are not recommended as a first-line drug but may be considered as an alternative for selected patients. While effective, there are differences in side effects. Also, resistance to fluoroquinolones is increasing.

Gepotidacin 1500 mg twice daily for 5 days is a new oral agent for UTI. In 2 noninferiority trials comparing it with nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily, it was noninferior and generally tolerated, although there were more discontinuations with gepotidacin and cost is higher.

An RCT enrolled women with UTI symptoms (76% culture positive, 60% symptoms for 2 or fewer days) and randomized them to ibuprofen 400 mg tid or a single dose of fosfomycin. Outcomes were slightly better for the women treated with antibiotics (1 day fewer symptoms, NNT fo cure at 4 days = 6) but not dramatically so. For women who wish to avoid an antibiotic, a closely monitored trial of an anti-inflammatory is an option.
A systematic review identified 5 RCTs comparing antibiotics with NSAIDs for acute uncomplicated UTI in women found an overall benefit for antibiotics.

A randomized trial in a family medicine clinic found that telehealth management of suspected UTI in women without signs of complications was safe and effective. A study in the setting of a commercial telehealth service, though, found that some high risk patients (over 65 years, signs of upper tract infection and men) were being treated empirically without culture.

Men: A 7- to 14-day course of TMP-SMX or a fluoroquinolone is an option for uncomplicated cystitis in young men. Nitrofurantoin and beta-lactams should not be used for cystitis in men because they do not achieve reliable tissue concentrations and are not effective for occult prostatitis.
Among afebrile men with suspected UTI, treatment with ciprofloxacin or TMP-SMX for seven days is non-inferior to a 14 day course.

For uncomplicated acute pyelonephritis, a 7-day course of ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily is recommended for empirical therapy in women when resistance locally does not exceed 10%. An initial 400 mg IV dose of ciprofloxacin may be used optionally. If local resistance to ciprofloxacin exceeds 10%, give an initial IV dose of ceftriaxone 1 gram or a consolidated 24 hour dose of an aminoglycoside.
If the pathogen is known to be susceptible, TMP-SMX 160/800 mg twice daily for 14 days is an acceptable alternative to ciprofloxacin for outpatient therapy of pyelonephritis.

Treatment of complicated UTI, such as in patients who have recently been hospitalized or instrumented, is similar to treatment of acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis. A randomized trial comparing piperacillin-tazobactam with meropenem-vaborbactam in 545 hospitalized patients with complicated UTI found no difference in clinical outcomes.

A study randomized 661 patients hospitalized with complicated UTI or pyelonephritis in a 2:1 ratioi to cefepime 2 gm + taniborbactam 0.5 gm (C-%) or meropenam 1 g, both given IV every 8 hours for at least 7 days and up to 14 days. For the subset of 436 patients with a susceptible gram negative pathogen, microbiologic cure was better with C-T (78.2% vs 66.4%, 95% CI for difference 2.9% to 21.0%) but not clinical cure (85.7% vs 81.1%, 95% CI for difference -2.6 to 12.6%). For the entire group of patients there was no difference in symptomatic clinical success (88.2% vs 87.7%).
A trial randomized hospitalized adults with complicated UTI (n=1372) to IV ertapenem or oral tebipenem pivoxil hydrobromide. The microbiologic and clinical cure rates were similar between drugs.

A systematic review of guidelines found lack of agreement between national guidelines for treatment of febrile UTI in men, with recommended antibiotic durations from 5 days (Scandanavia) to 10-14 days (most other countries). Most recommend use of a fluoroquinolone for febrile UTI in men.

A cluster randomized trial in 59 US hospitals randomized physicians to routine care or a computerized provider order entry (CPOE) that provided prompts regarding the risk of multidrug resistant organisms. It reduced use of extended spectrum antibiotics by 17% (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.77-0.89).

Hospitalization is recommended for moderate to severe cases of acute pyelonephritis (e.g., high fever, high white blood cell count, vomiting, dehydration, or evidence of sepsis). For patients with pyelonephritis requiring hospitalization, treat initially with IV antibiotics. Based on local resistance patterns, options include a fluoroquinonlone, an aminoglycoside plus ampicillin (optionally), a carbapenem, or a broad spectrum cephalosporin. After clinical improvement (usually 48-72 hours), the patient can be started on oral agents active against the infecting organism.

An RCT of 200 adults with febrile UTI compared 7 vs 14 days of antibiotics. There was no significant difference in outcomes between groups for women. Short-term outcomes were slightly worse for men with only 7 days of therapy, but long-term outcomes were similar. A more recent systematic review similarly found no difference between shorter and longer courses of antibiotics for uncomplicated UTI.

For women able to tolerate oral medications, there is no evidence that they are any less effective than parenterally administered antibiotics based on a systematic review of 15 RCTs with 1743 patients.

In hospitalized patients requiring a foley catheter, one to three doses of antibiotics at the time of catheter removal decreases the risk of subsequent UTI comparted to placebo (10.5% vs 4.7%, NNT = 17). Antibiotics tested included ciprofloxacin, co-trimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, and cefotaxime.

A randomized trial compared cefiderocol with imipenem-cilistatin in 450 patients hospitalized with acute complicated upper or lower UTI, or acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis. Patients without a gram negative pathogen were excluded and randomization was 2:1, so in the modified intention to treat analysis there were 252 receiving cefiderocol and 119 receiving imipenem-cilistatin. While a composite of clinical and microbiological cure was better in the cefiderocol group (73% vs 55%, p <0.05) but no significant difference between groups in early clinical response (90% vs 91%), end of treatment clinical response (98% vs 99%), or sustained clinical response (81% vs 72%, MD 9.0%, 95% CI -0.4-18.4).

A network meta-analysis compared carbapenem antibiotics with other antibiotics in hospitalized patients with complicated UTI. They found that meropenem/vaborbactam, ertapenem, and biapenem were more likely to be successful than carbapenems, while imipenem/cilastatin and meropenem/vaborbactam were more likely to cause adverse effects.
IDSA guidelines (2019) recommend that ASB should only be treated in pregnant women and in persons undergoing invasive urologic procedures.
The IDSA guidelines do not recommend treatment of ASB for healthy women, for persons with diabetes, for older women or men, and for persons with spinal cord injury or indwelling catheters.

Persons with both short-term and long-term indwelling urinary catheters (< 30 days) the guidelines do not recommend screening for or treating ASB. It is not known whether screening for ASB is helpful for patients at the time a catheter is removed. Antibiotics given at the time of catheter removal may prevent infection based on observational studies.

A systematic review identified only 4 studies with 652 participants comparing antibiotics with placebo for older adults with mental status changes/delirium and pyuria or bacteriuria. They found no benefit of antibiotics.

The efficacy of cranberry juice is questionable, with a 2007 Cochrane review concluding it has not been proven to be effective in the treatment of urinary tract infections, where as a recent meta-analysis concluded that cranberry-containing products (especially cranberry juice) are associated with protective effect against UTIs, especially in women with frequent recurrences (overall RRR = .38).
A cost analysis based on the results of an RCT found that in long term care facilities, cranberry capsules for patients at high risk fo UTI is unlikely to be cost-effective.
A systemic review and metanalysis found that D-mannose appears to be protective vs placebo for recurrent UTI in women over age 18, and is generally well tolerated.
Routine follow up for acute uncomplicated cystitis or acute pyelonephritis is not recommended if asymptomatic. C
More than 90% of women acute uncomplicated cystitis will become asymptomatic within 3 days after antimicrobial therapy. B

A systematic review identified 3 studies that followed adults with UTI who did not take an antimicrobial, typically the placebo group in a randomized trial. After 9 days, 42% reported that they were either symptom free or that symptoms had improved. However, by 6 weeks 39% of participants had still failed to improve.
The majority of UTIs in older men are considered complicated secondary to prostatic hypertrophy or genitourinary instrumentation.

While a longer course of treatment is often recommended, even for uncomplicated UTI, in older women, a systematic review of 15 studies found that short courses of 3 to 6 days were as effective as longer courses.
The rate of bacteriuria (2%-10%) and the infecting organisms are similar in pregnant and non-pregnant women.

All pregnant women should be screened for bacteriuria by urine culture at least once in early pregnancy (12-16 weeks gestation). A negative test for nitrites and leukocyte esterase rules out, and a positive test rules in infection in pregnant women.

Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy with antibiotics reduces the risk of pyelonephritis and low birthweight. Amoxicillin (pregnancy category B), nitrofurantoin (category B), sulfisoxazole (category C), cephalexin (category B), TMP-SMZ (category C), or amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (category B) are some of the recommended antibiotics. There is insufficient evidence to recommend one antibiotic over another.

The IDSA recommends a 3- to 7-day course of antibiotics for the treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy. Pregnant women should be screened periodically after the couirse of antibiotics for recurrent bacteriuria.
An RCT with 188 pregnant women found that cranberry juice did not prevent UTI.

cell.label: Urinary tract symptoms. Risk factors for complicated UTI, fever, or back pain?
Multiple symptoms consistent with UTI (frequency, dysuria, urgency)?
Test for nitrites and leukocyte esterase. Abnormal result?
Probable UTI; empiric therapy without urine culture. Telephone therapy acceptable. Symptoms resolve?
Pelvic examination; treat pathogens and consider urine culture.
Suspect pyelonephritis or high risk of treatment failure; urine culture and empiric therapy.
